name: NOVA
description: In many real-world applications, deployed models encounter inputs that differ from the data seen during training. Out-of-distribution detection identifies whether an input stems from an unseen distribution, while open-world recognition flags such inputs to ensure the system remains robust as ever-emerging, previously $unknown$ categories appear and must be addressed without retraining. Foundation and vision-language models are pre-trained on large and diverse datasets with the expectation of broad generalization across domains, including medical imaging. However, benchmarking these models on test sets with only a few common outlier types silently collapses the evaluation back to a closed-set problem, masking failures on rare or truly novel conditions encountered in clinical use. We therefore present $NOVA$, a challenging, real-life $evaluation-only$ benchmark of $\sim$900 brain MRI scans that span 281 rare pathologies and heterogeneous acquisition protocols. Each case includes rich clinical narratives and double-blinded expert bounding-box annotations. Together, these enable joint assessment of anomaly localisation, visual captioning, and diagnostic reasoning. Because NOVA is never used for training, it serves as an $extreme$ stress-test of out-of-distribution generalisation: models must bridge a distribution gap both in sample appearance and in semantic space. Baseline results with leading vision-language models (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Qwen2.5-VL-72B) reveal substantial performance drops across all tasks, establishing NOVA as a rigorous testbed for advancing models that can detect, localize, and reason about truly unknown anomalies.
evaluation_method: Task-specific metrics: localization (IoU / mAP), captioning (BLEU / CIDEr), reasoning (accuracy / F1)
general_score_metric: Task-specific composite (IoU/mAP for localization; BLEU/CIDEr for captioning; accuracy/F1 for reasoning)
reputation: An emerging, rigorous medical imaging stress-test adopted by researchers evaluating V‑L and OOD performance on rare clinical anomalies.
notes: Small evaluation-only dataset (~900 scans) with many rare pathologies; not intended for training. Sensitive medical data and annotation biases possible; performance varies widely across tasks and cases.
